description_full: Verra Mobility Corporation provides smart mobility technology solutions in the United States, Australia, Europe, and Canada. It operates through three segments: Commercial Services, Government Solutions, and Parking Solutions. The Commercial Services segment offers automated toll and violations management, and title and registration solutions to rental car companies, direct commercial fleet owner-operators, fleet management companies, and other fleet owners. The Government Solutions segment provides photo enforcement solutions and services to its customers, including complete, end-to-end speed, red-light, and school bus stop arm and bus lane enforcement solutions; and traffic enforcement products and recurring maintenance services related to the equipment and software. This segment serves municipalities, counties, school districts, and law enforcement agencies. The Parking Solutions segment offers an integrated suite of parking software, transaction processing and hardware solutions to its customers, which include universities, municipalities, healthcare facilities, and commercial parking operators. This segment also develops specialized hardware and parking management software that provides a platform for the issuance of parking permits, enforcement, gateless vehicle counting, and event parking and citation services, as well as produces and markets its proprietary software as a service to its customers. The company was founded in 1987 and is headquartered in Mesa, Arizona.

financial_summary: Verra Mobility Corporation is a small-cap technology business with a $333M market cap on $133M of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +12% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder. Operating margins are expanding by +25.1pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 9% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically.

The business throws off $137M in free cash flow — roughly 103 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.87× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.7× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 3.7×.

Management returns a meaningful 40.1% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and stock-based comp at 19% of revenue is silent dilution an owner has to account for, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 7.7× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

prof: ROIC of 9% earns above the cost of capital of 8.0%, but the 1pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.60).
It converts 103% of revenue into free cash flow, or 84% after stock compensation.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 8/9 and cash conversion of 1.87x.
ROE of 47% is amplified by 5.6x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.

hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.7x net debt to EBITDA ($65.3M of cash against $1.0B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 3.7x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 0.67 in the distress zone, which caps the rating at HOLD.
Goodwill makes up 45% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 12.1% over 3 years and -19.5% over 5 years, so growth is accelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 37%).
At current returns, reinvesting 25% of profits supports about 2.2% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 43.3% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 0.55 (orders lagging sales), a backlog worth 1.1x annual revenue and deferred revenue down 9%.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.0x, 89.6% of sales), a maintenance pace.
own: Insiders own a modest 1.1%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
It returns 40.1% a year to shareholders (40.1% in buybacks).
The share count has shrunk 1.1% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
people: With about 1,888 employees, each generates about $70K of revenue, 0.2x the Technology median, and productivity has fallen 13.6% a year.
That works out to $72K of free cash flow per employee.
